source.title: Why Spectral Normalization Stabilizes GANs: Analysis and Improvements
source.authors: Zinan Lin; V. Sekar; G. Fanti

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies gradient stability and sample quality in GAN training, but does not measure training classification error or test any listed version’s specific claim.
record.gate_note: The reported GAN gradient norms and sample-quality outcomes concern related training behavior, but do not establish whether the classification networks in the claim reach near-zero training error.
record.test_reason: The study uses initialization principles underlying V4 to design spectral normalization methods, then measures GAN gradients and sample quality. It does not test initialization effects on learning speed or trainable depth, or any other listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors provide theoretical bounds and empirical evidence connecting spectral normalization to control of exploding and vanishing discriminator gradients, and report improved GAN sample quality and stability with BSSN. They explicitly acknowledge that gradient control may be only one contributor to spectral normalization's success.
record.recipe_differences: Studies spectral normalization and its variants in GAN training, not gradient-based classification training from random initialization.
record.method_sensitivity: The normalization implementation matters: the paper reports vanishing gradients for strict SNConv and stable gradients for SNw. Scaling SNConv by 1.75 gives similar gradients and inception score to SNw in the reported CIFAR10 comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: In CIFAR10 GAN training, SNw maintains stable parameter variance and hinge-loss gradients, whereas removing SN produces increasing variance and decreasing gradients. Unscaled strict SNConv produces vanishing discriminator-output gradients; scaling it by 1.75 yields gradients and sample quality similar to SNw.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Spectral-normalization implementation and scaling affect gradient stability and sample quality during GAN training.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling LeCun initialization changes peak GAN inception score, with favorable modes around 0.2 and 1.2 in the CIFAR10 experiment (Section 5.2, Figure 8; Appendix M).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialization scale affects GAN sample quality, with multiple favorable scaling regimes under the tested adversarial-training recipe.

record.problems: The study measures GAN sample quality and gradient norms rather than classification training error. Several gradient results are shown only in figures, without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows retained. Other GAN sample-quality comparisons, including the SN/BSN benchmark tables and scaling sweeps, concern the paper’s proposed GAN normalization method and do not measure the classification-training behavior in the claim.

untested.parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including random labels, and its dependence on capacity or training recipe.
Spurious local minima in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and their dependence on excess student width.
Depth-dependent training error in plain networks versus networks with identity shortcuts, and the specified initialization exceptions.

Effects of activation-matched initialization on learning speed and trainable depth; orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization; very deep plain convolutional networks. The LeCun scaling sweep measures peak GAN sample quality instead.
Loss recovery, curvature evolution and divergence relative to measured learning-rate stability thresholds.
Controlled batch-normalization comparisons for training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and comparisons with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: Initialization findings are substantively used, making T4 more appropriate than T6. Gradient stability alone does not establish V4's learning-speed or trainable-depth claims. Batch normalization is used in generators, but its effect is not isolated.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 classification error, random or corrupted labels, network size, optimizer, and training duration.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student networks, spurious minima, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual classification networks, depth effects on training error, and shortcut comparisons.
Activation-matched initializations and their effect on plain-network learning speed or trainable depth.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, loss recovery, sharpness, and divergence in the specified settings.
Batch normalization’s effect on accuracy speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

rows.subject: GAN discriminator on CIFAR10
rows.size_stated: Architecture in Tables 2 and 3; discriminator has seven convolutional layers and a final fully connected layer.
rows.operation_detail: Compared discriminator gradient norms during GAN training with and without spectral normalization.
rows.note: The text states that with SN, gradient magnitude is stable; without SN, parameter variance rises and gradient magnitude quickly decreases. Figure values are not transcribed.
rows.check: Appendix L.2 uses popular SNw, not strict SNConv. Figure 18 measures the parameter gradient norm of the real-sample hinge-loss term, ReLU(1 − D(real)); Figure 19 measures inception score. The strict-SN comparison concerning exploding gradients belongs to Appendix J, Figure 13. These outcomes do not determine any listed version.

rows.subject: SNConv (Farnia et al.)
rows.operation_detail: Measured gradient norms while training GANs with strict spectral normalization.
rows.note: The text says SNConv gradients vanish during CIFAR10 training, while SNw gradients remain stable. Inception score is also shown, but no precise figure values are stated in the prose.
rows.check: The reported vanishing of SNConv gradients relative to stable SNw gradients is accurate, but 'absent' cannot describe a listed claim's effect here. Figure 5 measures gradients of D(real); Figure 4 separately measures inception score. Neither tests a listed version.

rows.subject: SN (Miyato et al.) discriminator
rows.size_stated: Architecture in Tables 2 and 3; discriminator has seven convolutional layers and a final fully connected layer.
rows.operation_detail: Tracked parameter variance and gradient magnitude during GAN training with SN.
rows.measure: Parameter variance and gradient magnitude over training
rows.value: Parameter variance is described as stable throughout training; gradient magnitude is described as stable.
rows.note: The text describes these trends; the figures do not provide values transcribed in the prose.
rows.check: The stated stability is supported, but it does not determine any listed version. Split parameter variance (Figure 17) from the parameter gradient norm of ReLU(1 − D(real)) (Figure 18). The gradient measure is a hinge-loss gradient, rather than simply the gradient of the discriminator output.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
